submissive

sub-MISS-iv -- three syllables, stress on the second syllable, MISS. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Submissive is ready to obey the will of others.

Rather than defend her own idea, the submissive assistant nodded along with everything the manager said.

Example

Whenever his lab partner announces a plan, the submissive boy shelves his own ideas, shrugs, and says 'whatever you want' -- even when he is sure the experiment will fail.

Submissive means setting aside your own will and yielding to someone else's -- actively giving way to another person's wishes, often at the cost of your own.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

yielding: Yielding means giving way when pushed -- a yielding person bends to pressure in the moment. Submissive goes deeper: a standing readiness to obey another person's will, even before any pressure arrives. Someone can be yielding in one argument without being submissive by nature.

passive: Passive means simply letting things happen without acting or resisting -- there may be no one giving orders at all. Submissive is active in its own way: it bows to a particular person's will. A passive viewer just watches; a submissive assistant obeys.

unassertive: Unassertive means failing to put your own views forward -- staying quiet in the meeting. Submissive goes a step further: not just silent about your will, but ready to set it aside and follow someone else's. An unassertive person hides an opinion; a submissive one surrenders it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defiant: openly resisting authority

assertive: confidently standing up for oneself

Where it sits · how far your own will fades

deferential → submissive → servile

deferential vs. submissive: Deferential is politer and healthier than submissive -- a deferential junior lawyer yields to the senior partner's judgment out of respect, while a submissive one has stopped voicing judgments of her own at all.

servile vs. submissive: Servile goes further than submissive: a submissive person gives way to another's will, but a servile one grovels -- eager to obey before being asked, as if serving were the whole of who they are.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sub-: under (Latin)

Root — miss: to send, to let go (from Latin mittere; it appears as -mit in transmit and as miss- here)

Suffix — -ive: having the quality of (Latin -ivus)

Put it together: Submissive builds on Latin submittere: sub- ('under') + miss (from mittere, 'to send') + -ive ('having the quality of') -- 'sending or placing oneself under.' A submissive person does exactly that: they lower their own will underneath someone else's.

Use the root in a new word: transmit: The station transmits the weather forecast every hour on the hour.

Word Building

Word Choice

Submissive describes yielding one's own will to someone else's: a submissive posture, a submissive reply. It often carries an uneasy shade -- healthy respect is deferential, but a submissive person may be giving up too much. Docile, by contrast, is a naturally mild temperament, and compliant is about following rules rather than people.
